title: Final boss of solo game development: marketing
author: algorys
selftext:
Funny thing I discovered when releasing my game: apparently, making the game was only the first part of making a game.

Then comes the second boss: marketing. 😂

I've spent almost a year and a half working on this project: coding, designing the mechanics, writing the story, building the world, balancing things, fixing bugs... and finally creating all the assets, which I made using AI.

I somehow managed to find almost 100 people willing to test it, had around 30 daily active players during testing, survived Google's testing requirements, and finally got approved for production on the Play Store.

And then...

"Oh. Right. Now people actually need to know the game exists."

Welcome to marketing. 😂

And of course, because I used AI for the visual assets, I've also discovered the AI-hater part of releasing a game.

I completely understand that there's a mountain of low-effort AI-generated games appearing everywhere. Generate some assets, copy an existing mechanic, throw everything together and call it a game.

But I think we're starting to confuse two different questions:

"Was AI used to make this game?"

and

"Is this actually a good game?"

AI doesn't create an interesting game automatically. It doesn't magically give you good mechanics, an interesting world, meaningful choices or months of balancing and debugging.

And on the other side, not using AI doesn't magically make a game good either.

We've had uninspired AAA games, predatory mobile games, endless clones, energy systems, microtransaction factories and €70 disappointments long before generative AI existed.

As a solo developer, AI allowed me to create visual assets for a game that I simply couldn't have afforded otherwise.

I'm not pretending those assets were hand-painted by an artist. They weren't. I used AI, and I'm perfectly open about it.

But behind them there's still a game I've spent roughly 18 months designing and building.

So maybe the useful question isn't:

AI or no AI?

Maybe it's:

Is there actually a game worth playing behind those assets?

Anyway, apparently I now have to learn marketing.

I preferred debugging. 😂

replies.author: AutomaticTalent
replies.body:
When TETRIS walked through the door at Brøderbund Software in 1985 it was basic characters which fell to the bottom immediately when you hit the space bar.

Productivity at the company stopped for three full days while we "evaluated" the game, but it was clear from the first touch - this game was fundamentally fun.

The original Lode Runner has a similar appeal, simple game play, simple graphics, basic audio, no flash - but all game.  Plus a level editor, in 1983!

comments.author: AutomaticTalent
comments.body:
I am also a musician, and this is a common challenge for musicians creating their original music.

When digital audio workstations became available to the masses, people put together all their music, but then they didn’t know what to do with it and it still exists. 

Marketing and promotion are just one more piece of the big puzzle.

I put together a little radar graph on my website so that new developers could check to see where they might need some help.

comments.author: Arkenhammer
comments.body:
So here's the deal with marketing: players decide to buy your game by comparing it to their other options. Roughly at the moment that means a first impression that is in the top 5% of games on your market of choice.

The market I know best it Steam; there's roughly 1000 successful games on Steam every year. That number doesn't change much from year to year. Typically there's about 20000 new games published each year but AI tools getting better have opened the floodgates. Say next year there are 30000 new games on steam, 10000 of them made with AI. There will still only be 1000 successful games because, roughly, that is the size of the market. AI isn't increasing the size of the market, it is raising the bar. Those 10000 new games, to the average consumer, all look the same and fall to the bottom. This is what AI slop really means: it's not that the games are bad, it is that they like everything else.

The question isn't about which tools you use. It is whether you can make something rises above the crowd and looks more appealing than 30000 other developers all trying to do the same thing.

comments.author: imnotabot303
comments.body:
What you are talking about won't go away. People will always dislike something due to how it was made based on their personal ethics or morals.

A burger can taste good but it doesn't make the burger industry good.

On top of that AI will always be associated with less skill and lower effort as well as faster development time and cheaper costs.

With any product, if it requires less skill and has faster, cheaper production costs you expect the price to reflect it. No matter how good the game is there's always going to be people that will have a problem if the AI game is priced as highly as a none AI game.

Plus getting you game seen is only going to get harder and harder as AI gets better because there will be more and more competition.
